Hyper-Charismatic
HY-per kair-iz-MAT-ik
adjective (extreme charismatic excess)
From “hyper-” (excessive) and “charismatic” (of the spiritual gifts, Greek charismata); the extreme wing of the charismatic movement marked by unbridled claims of prophecy, miracle, and revelation.

📖 Biblical Definition

“Hyper-charismatic” describes the extreme wing of the charismatic and Pentecostal movement, marked by unbridled and unaccountable claims of prophecy, miracle, new revelation, and apostolic authority—as in the New Apostolic Reformation, certain “signs and wonders” ministries, and movements such as Bethel and the Toronto phenomenon. The dictionary, holding the cessationist Reformed position, distinguishes this excess both from the historic Reformed faith and from the more sober charismatic believers who, though continuationist, hold to Scripture's authority and order. The marks of the hyper-charismatic are these: prophecies and “words from the Lord” that add to or rival Scripture and are seldom tested or held accountable when they fail; claims of miracles and healings unverified and often manifestly false; chaotic and ecstatic worship that the apostle's rule would forbid, for God is not the author of confusion but of peace; and self-styled apostles and prophets claiming an authority the closed canon does not allow. The dictionary marks the movement against the plain commands of Scripture. Believers are to try the spirits, whether they are of God, for many false prophets are gone out into the world; they are to beware of those who turn away their ears from the truth unto fables; and they are warned by the Lord that many will claim to have prophesied and done wonderful works in His name, to whom He will say, “I never knew you.” The dictionary does not deny the reality of the Spirit's work or counsel a dead formalism; it insists that the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures does not contradict or add to them, that all things in worship be done decently and in order, and that every claim to prophecy, miracle, and revelation be tested by the Word of God, the closed and sufficient canon.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The extreme wing of the charismatic movement, marked by unaccountable claims of prophecy, miracle, and new revelation (NAR, Bethel, Toronto); rejected for adding to Scripture and breeding confusion, against the commands to try the spirits and do all things in order.

HYPER-CHARISMATIC, adjective. [Greek charismata, gifts.] The extreme, unaccountable wing of the charismatic movement.

Marked by prophecies and “words” that rival or add to Scripture, seldom tested.

By unverified miracle-claims and chaotic, ecstatic worship.

By self-styled apostles and prophets the closed canon does not allow.

Against the commands to try the spirits (1 John 4:1) and do all things in order (1 Corinthians 14:33).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Co 14:33 — "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints."

1 Jo 4:1 — "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."

Mt 7:22 — "Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?"

2 Ti 4:4 — "And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Hyper-charismatic excess is itself the corruption: it adds to Scripture by unaccountable prophecy, breeds confusion in worship, and exalts self-styled apostles and unverified miracles against the closed and sufficient canon.

expand to see more

The hyper-charismatic excess is the corruption to be named. It floods the church with prophecies and “words from the Lord” that add to or rival the closed canon and are rarely tested or repented of when they fail; it parades unverified and often manifestly false miracles; it fosters chaotic, ecstatic worship that the apostle's rule forbids, for God is not the author of confusion but of peace; and it raises up self-styled apostles and prophets claiming an authority that ended with the foundation-laying apostles. The dictionary, holding the cessationist position, names this a grave departure from Scripture's authority and order.

Yet the dictionary is careful in its distinctions. It does not equate every charismatic believer with the hyper-charismatic fringe; many continuationists hold to the authority of Scripture and the order of worship and are brethren in the gospel. Nor does it counsel a dead formalism that quenches the Spirit. Its insistence is this: the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures neither contradicts nor adds to them; believers are commanded to try the spirits, for many false prophets are gone out into the world; and the Lord Himself warned that many will boast of prophecies and wonders done in His name, to whom He will say, “I never knew you.” Every claim to prophecy, miracle, and revelation must be tested by the Word of God, the closed and all-sufficient canon, and all things in worship done decently and in order.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From “hyper-” (Greek, over, excessive) and “charismatic” (from charismata, gifts of grace); the excess of the charismatic movement beyond the bounds of Scripture and order.

expand to see more

Hyper, Greek, “over” or “beyond,” marking excess.

Charismata, Greek, “gifts of grace,” the spiritual gifts.

Associated with the New Apostolic Reformation, Bethel, and the Toronto phenomenon.

Marked by untested prophecy, unverified miracle, and chaotic worship.

Distinguished from sober continuationists who hold Scripture's authority.

Usage

"The pastor warned against hyper-charismatic prophecy that adds to the closed and sufficient Scripture."

"He distinguished the sober continuationist brother from the unaccountable hyper-charismatic fringe."

"She tried the spirits by the Word, refusing the unverified wonders paraded in Christ's name."
